text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)

THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW In a result that has quashed hopes of another cut in interest rates, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday indicate the economic recovery is broadening. Retail sales rose by an unexpectedly large 2.7 per cent in January after seasonaladjustment and building approvals jumped by 10.4 per cent in the same month. Page 1.

Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer has bowed to pressure over the Papua New Guinea affair and has cancelled a trip to Mauritius. Downer announced he will be replaced by Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer. Cabinet has reached no formal decision on ow to respond to Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's threat to use mercenaries to wipe out the rebel uprising in his country. Page 2.

Liberal Senator Bob Woods has announced he will resign from the Senate at the end of the week, after he successfully found a 'pair' for the upcoming vote on euthanasia. He announced last night he had come to an agreement with fellow Senator Winston Crane who had intended to vote against Kevin Andrew's bill. Page 2.

The Federal Government has backed down on several key regulatory changes for the up-coming one-third privatisation of Telstra, which is likely to increase costs and restrict its ability to compete in the de-regulated market. The Government is likely to anounce plans to extend its untimed local call service for both voice and data services to business. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

It has been revealed that shortly after announcing his intention to resign from politics last month, Senator Bob Woods, who is under investigation by the Australian Federal Police over allegations of rorting his parliamentary perks, approached the Finance Department to ask whether he was entitled to claim a generous taxpayer-funded pension for life - including on the grounds of ill-health. Page 1.

Embattled Queensland Senator Mal Colston has dismissed new allegations, including that he flew to Perth and back without leaving the airport to accrue frequent-flyer points and that he asked the parliamentary library to do his son's university homework, ad last night claimed the allegations could involve criminal breaches of privacy legislation. Page 1.

Despite Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's promise to work for a "political solution" to the Bougainville conflict, the Federal Cabinet and the six-member National Security Committee met on Monday and again yesterday to decide upon an actio plan to force PNG to abandon the use of foreign mercenaries. Page 1.

On the first day of his jury trial in the Queensland Supreme Court yesterday, charity worker Paul Wade Streeton admitted he intended to inflict grievous bodily harm on six-year-old Tjandamurra O'Shane by igniting him with petrol in a Cairns schoolyard in ctober. Streeton told police he had been planning such an attack since he was in grade two. Page 1.

THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD Following a proposal aimed at addressing the storage problem for 1,600 spent fuel rods from the 38-year-old research reactor at Lucas Heights in Sydney's southern suburbs by reprocessing in Australia rather than overseas, Federal Cabinet is investigating he construction of a nuclear waste reprocessing plant at the site. Page 1.

After announcing last week the setting up of a major task force to try and catch a serial rapist wanted for attacks on 29 Sydney women, the Commander of Crime Agencies, Assistant Commissioner Clive Small admitted yesterday police had bungled the investigaion into the rapist. Small said police had lost critical evidence, including more than one semen sample. Page 1.

Paul Wade Streeton, a 27-year-old charity worker accused of setting fire to a boy in a Cairns schoolyard, yesterday pleaded guilty in the Cairns Supreme Court to grievous bodily harm with intent, but not guilty to attempted murder charges arising from theattack. The court heard yesterday Streeton had been planning the attack since Year 2 and wanted the death penalty for the act. Page 1.

Millions of dollars worth of milk and processed meat products have been left stranded on wharves and ships following a decision by South Korean health officials last week to freeze meat and dairy exports from Australia in the wake of Victoria's anthrax oubreak. Page 1.
THE AGE

Australian officials are deeply troubled by a decision by South Korea - Australia's second-largest meat and dairy export market - to freeze imports after Victoria's anthrax outbreak. The freeze, which some officials believe is partially politically motivaed, was imposed last week by South Korean health officials by kept quiet by Australian officials. Page 1.

While data released yesterday by the Australian Bureau of Statistics supports the Federal Government's claims that the economy is picking up, with building approvals for new housing rising 10 per cent and retail sales soaring in January, economists have wrned that the results are not all they seemed. Page 1.

Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer, who has been embroiled in a row with High Court Chief Justice Sir Gerald Brennan over political criticism of the Wik decision, said yesterday he wants a "capital C Conservative" to replace Brennan when he retires next yer. Page 1.

The Supreme Court heard yesterday the Victorian Department of Human Services had planned for six months to take a baby from its intellectually disabled mother after she gave birth. Hartog Berkley QC told the court the Department had used a "jack-boot appoach" reminiscent of Hitler's Germany when it took the mother's baby only minutes after the birth. Page A3.
